subject: Agriculture
title: From Villages to Cities
description: A fast breakdown of From Villages to Cities for builders.

hook.text: Farming created food surpluses. Surpluses let some people stop farming—and start doing other things.

buildup.text: Specialists emerged: potters, weavers, priests, soldiers. None of them grew their own food.

discovery.text: Villages grew into towns, then cities. Jericho had a thousand residents by 8000 BCE.

twist.text: Surpluses also created inequality. Those who controlled the grain controlled everyone else.

climax.text: Writing itself was invented to track grain stores. The first documents were farm receipts.

punchline.text: Civilization began with a surplus of wheat.

quiz.question: What was the primary purpose of the earliest writing systems?
options: Tracking grain stores and agricultural records

details.summary: The transition from villages to cities was driven by agricultural surpluses that freed people from farming to become artisans, merchants, and rulers. This topic connects food production to urbanization and the birth of complex societies.
details.whyItMatters: Without farming surpluses, cities could never have formed. Understanding this link reveals why food production capacity has always determined the size and complexity of human civilizations.
takeaways: Agricultural surpluses enabled specialization of labor beyond food production
Early cities like Uruk depended on surrounding farmland to feed dense populations
Grain storage and distribution systems were among the first government functions

faq.question: How did agriculture lead to the development of cities?
faq.answer: Farming produced food surpluses that supported non-farming specialists—potters, builders, priests, and administrators. Concentrating these specialists together created permanent settlements that grew into villages and eventually into the first cities.

faq.question: What role did grain storage play in early civilizations?
faq.answer: Grain storage allowed communities to survive between harvests and through poor years. Managing grain reserves required accounting, record-keeping, and administration—driving the development of writing, bureaucracy, and centralized governance.
